chunks.answer: Face Unlock for Windows 11 is one of my most technically ambitious personal projects. Its goal is to provide native face-based authentication directly at the Windows 11 lock screen, rather than being a normal standalone face-recognition application. I like this project because it sits at the boundary between application software and the operating system — taking several different technologies and making them work together to solve a problem that a simple application alone can't solve.

chunks.answer: The system combines a C++ Windows Credential Provider with a Python biometric daemon. The C++ side is implemented as a Windows Credential Provider using Win32 and COM, while the Python side performs the biometric processing. The two processes communicate through Windows Named Pipes.

chunks.answer: The project became significantly more complicated than a normal computer-vision demo because it had to work with actual Windows system behavior. Some of the difficult problems I encountered included process isolation, Python PATH conflicts, virtual environments and interpreter environments, model loading speed, boot-time race conditions, inter-process communication, Windows authentication, and overall system reliability. A particularly important part was dealing with boot-time race conditions and environment initialization so the system could behave reliably from a cold boot.

chunks.answer: The Siri chatbot's knowledge base is stored as structured, answer-sized chunks. I'm building the retrieval system locally using Python, TF-IDF, and cosine similarity, using question patterns, keywords, topics, and answers so the system can find the most relevant information before passing it to a language model. The generation layer is intended to use Groq. The system is intentionally lightweight and explainable rather than immediately using a vector database or a complicated retrieval stack.

chunks.answer: I implemented authentication simulation using JSON mock data and React hooks for session management. The tech stack includes React.js, React Router DOM, JavaScript, CSS3, localStorage, and JSON mock data. Instead of a real backend, login is simulated by checking credentials against JSON data using JavaScript array methods, and after a successful login the user object is stored in localStorage. React's useState and useEffect hooks manage dynamic state such as the selected class, student lists, and attendance status. When attendance is submitted, records are appended to an array and stored under the attendanceRecords key in localStorage, and when students log in, their history is filtered using their roll number and class code. The UI uses a clean card-based responsive design with custom CSS.

chunks.answer: I worked on a content-based game recommendation system using a Steam games dataset, as a collaborative effort with Satwik Maurya and Abhishek Yadav. Its purpose is to recommend games based on a user's natural-language description of the type of gaming experience they want, analyzing game descriptions, genres, ratings, and community tags rather than requiring users to know specific game names or navigate filters manually.

chunks.answer: The Game Recommender uses content-based filtering, comparing a user's description against game attributes and ranking games by how closely they match. It's built with Python, Pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, and NLP tooling such as NLTK or spaCy. A TF-IDF Vectorizer converts textual game information into numerical representations, and cosine similarity compares user prompts against the processed game data. The project also includes data preprocessing and feature engineering, cleaning the dataset to retain relevant English-language information and useful fields like descriptions, genres, ratings, and tags.

chunks.answer: I am Shreshtha Sharma, also known as Siri, a BCA student specializing in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence at Shri Ramswaroop Memorial University. My journey into technology was unconventional — I chose Biology in Class XII while my family expected me to pursue medicine, took a gap year to prepare for NEET and scored 438 marks, but ultimately realized technology was the direction I wanted, so I chose BCA.
